---
title: "Conditional probability"
---

The joint probability $\mathbb{P}(N,O)$ is computed relative to the full token extract. Suppose instead we ask: among tokens whose lemma is *ne*, what proportion are annotated `obj`? The phrase *among the* changes the reference event.

Basically, conditioning keeps only the mass inside a reference event and rescales it to sum to one. More specifically, for events $B,C\in\mathcal F$ with $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$, the [**conditional probability**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html) of $B$ given $C$ is

$$
\mathbb{P}(B\mid C)
\equiv
\frac{\mathbb{P}(B,C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}.
$$

The denominator identifies the reference event; the numerator identifies the part of that event for which the target event also occurs.

```{r}
#| label: load-conditional-data
library(ggplot2)

wh <- read.csv(
  "data/ud-turkish-boun/question-core-arguments.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  fileEncoding = "UTF-8"
)

stopifnot(nrow(wh) == 167L)

is_ne <- as.logical(wh$ne_lemma)
is_object <- as.logical(wh$object)
p_ne <- mean(is_ne)
p_object <- mean(is_object)
p_ne_object <- mean(is_ne & is_object)

p_object_given_ne <- p_ne_object / p_ne
p_ne_given_object <- p_ne_object / p_object

stopifnot(
  p_ne > 0,
  p_object > 0,
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    p_object_given_ne,
    mean(is_object[is_ne])
  )),
  isTRUE(all.equal(
    p_ne_given_object,
    mean(is_ne[is_object])
  ))
)

c(object_given_ne = p_object_given_ne,
  ne_given_object = p_ne_given_object)
```

## Conditioning as rescaling

Let $N$ be the *ne* event and $O$ the object event. Then

$$
\mathbb{P}(O\mid N)
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(O,N)}{\mathbb{P}(N)}.
$$

The empirical value is `r round(p_object_given_ne, 3)`. The conditional complement follows from the same rescaling:

$$
\mathbb{P}(O^c\mid N)
=
1-\mathbb{P}(O\mid N).
$$

```{r}
#| label: check-conditional-complement
p_subject_given_ne <- mean(
  wh$dependency_relation[is_ne] == "nsubj"
)

stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(
  p_object_given_ne + p_subject_given_ne,
  1
)))

c(object = p_object_given_ne, subject = p_subject_given_ne)
```

Conditioning also makes its own reference event certain:

$$
\mathbb{P}(C\mid C)
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(C,C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(C)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}
=1.
$$

## Reversing target and condition

The reversed probability uses the same intersection but a different denominator:

$$
\mathbb{P}(N\mid O)
=
\frac{\mathbb{P}(N,O)}{\mathbb{P}(O)}.
$$

Its empirical value is `r round(p_ne_given_object, 3)`. Thus $\mathbb{P}(O\mid N)$ and $\mathbb{P}(N\mid O)$ answer different linguistic questions even though they share a numerator.

```{r}
#| label: plot-conditional-probabilities
#| fig-cap: "Observed dependency-relation proportions within each lemma. Bars rescale separately within lemma."
conditional_counts <- as.data.frame(
  xtabs(~ lemma + dependency_relation, data = wh)
)
names(conditional_counts)[3] <- "tokens"
conditional_counts$conditional_probability <- ave(
  conditional_counts$tokens,
  conditional_counts$lemma,
  FUN = function(x) x / sum(x)
)

ggplot(conditional_counts,
       aes(lemma, conditional_probability, fill = dependency_relation)) +
  geom_col(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(nsubj = "grey", obj = "steelblue")) +
  labs(x = "Annotated lemma",
       y = "Conditional probability within lemma",
       fill = "UD relation") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Positive-probability conditions

The ratio definition requires $\mathbb{P}(C)>0$. If the conditioning event has zero probability, the denominator is zero and the elementary conditional probability is undefined. All three lemma events have positive mass in the observed extract, as the raw bars show.

The conditional values remain descriptions of this filtered treebank population. A difference among lemma-specific object proportions may reflect syntax, lexical semantics, register composition, annotation, or their combination. Conditioning changes a denominator; it does not identify a causal account.

Conditioning changes the reference event and renormalizes its mass. The [next page](probability-factorization.qmd) rearranges the definition to recover a joint probability from a conditional and a marginal probability.

## Check your understanding

1. Compute $\mathbb{P}(O^c\mid N)$ from the raw rows and with the complement rule.
2. Compute $\mathbb{P}(O\mid L=\textit{kim})$ and $\mathbb{P}(L=\textit{kim}\mid O)$. Explain their denominators.
3. Verify directly that conditioning $N$ on itself returns the certain-event probability in the empirical measure.
4. Which scientific claims remain unsupported by the observed difference among lemma-specific object proportions?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. $\mathbb{P}(O^c\mid N)=35/147=0.238095$, which also equals $1-112/147$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. $\mathbb{P}(O\mid L=\textit{kim})=3/17=0.176471$ uses 17 *kim* tokens as its denominator; $\mathbb{P}(L=\textit{kim}\mid O)=3/116=0.025862$ uses 116 object tokens. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. $\mathbb{P}(N\mid N)=147/147=1$ because filtering the *ne* rows by the same *ne* condition retains every row. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. The observed lemma-specific object proportions do not identify syntax, lexical semantics, register, or annotation as a cause because the treebank did not manipulate or balance those explanations. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>
